# The Master's Eye

*A farm on the Campanian plain, late September. The wheat is already in the horreum; the vines are being picked. An old farmer named Vettius, who works eight iugera with two oxen and a nephew, is mending a basket in the shade of a fig tree when a stranger asks for water and stays to talk.*

---

"Eight iugera," Vettius says, "and I know every furrow of them the way a man knows his own hands. Where the ground stays cold in spring. Which corner the north wind scours. Where the moles come through." He taps his temple. "That is my almanac."

The stranger nods. "And if I told you a farmer of my country carries the same knowledge — for two hundred iugera — in a stone the size of a fig?"

"Then I would say you come from a country of liars or of gods."

"Neither. Only of better instruments."

---

**On knowing the field.**

"Tell me first how you decide where to sow," the stranger says, "and where to let the land rest."

"By tasting the earth," Vettius says, unbothered. "By the weeds that grow in it. By whether it holds water in February. Columella says as much and Columella was no fool."

"Then you already think in maps. You simply keep them in your head, in a single copy, which sleeps when you sleep and dies with you. We make them outside the head — the whole farm drawn in strips, each one measured for how much water it holds, how much nitrogen it lacks, how deep the good soil runs. The ploughman's boy carries the map in his hand and sees which strip wants lime and which wants nothing."

Vettius's knife pauses. "And the map knows better than the man who has walked the strip for forty years?"

"Sometimes. It knows the strip in a dry year and a wet year and the year the hail came, all at once, and it never forgets one of them. You have seen forty harvests. It has seen forty thousand, from farms you will never visit."

---

**On water.**

"Water is the whole argument," Vettius says. "A man can lose a crop in ten days of the wrong weather. My grandfather dug the channel from the stream, and we open the gate and let it run, and God decides the rest."

"We measure it. Little vessels buried in the soil that tell you, at any hour, how thirsty the roots are. Not the surface — the roots, a forearm down. And instead of drowning the field, we give each plant a slow thread of water at its foot, so that a third of the water does the work of all of it. In a dry summer that is the difference between borrowing money and not."

"And who reads these buried vessels?"

"The farmer. Or the vessel speaks to his little tablet and the tablet says, *the third field is dry, the fourth is not.*" The stranger smiles. "It is a very obedient nomenclator."

---

**On blight, and on Robigus.**

"Then there is the rust," Vettius says, and his voice changes. "The red dust on the wheat. You will laugh, but we keep the Robigalia, and we lead the puppy and the sheep around the fields, because what else is there to do? You see a spot on a leaf and by the time you have told your neighbour, the field is orange and the year is gone."

"We do not laugh. We lost a great deal to rust before we learned to see it early. Now a boy walks the field with a little box that looks at leaves faster than any man's eye and says, *this one has it, that one does not, and this one will have it in four days.* Then we treat the few plants, not the field. We also read the wind, and the wetness on the leaves at dawn, and we say to a whole district, *the rust is coming from the south, cut your hay early.*"

"Four days' warning." Vettius looks at the horizon for a while. "My father would have wept for four days' warning."

---

**On beasts, and on weather.**

"Your cattle — do you know when a cow will calve?"

"Usually. Not always. We lost a cow last spring because she chose a night in the rain and no one walked the byre."

"A collar the weight of a bracelet counts her steps and her chewing, and notices before she does that the day is coming. It tells you at dusk: *tonight, the black one, watch her.* And it tells you when a beast is sick before the beast will admit it, because a cow is proud and hides her fever until she cannot."

"And the weather?"

"Here I must be humble. We cannot command the sky. We can only guess better. We gather the readings from ten thousand farms — the wind, the pressure, the wetness — and we say, *rain in three days, and it will be heavy.* Not always right. But right often enough that a man cuts his hay on Tuesday instead of Thursday, and the hay is dry."

Vettius laughs, short and genuine. "The geese. We listen to the geese. My wife swears by the geese."

"Keep the geese. Ours are less reliable than ours are expensive."

---

**On the market, and on the voice in the hand.**

"One more thing," the stranger says. "The hardest question on a farm is not *how* to grow. It is *what* to grow, and *when* to sell."

"Ah." Vettius sets the basket down. "There you have the true god of the countryside — the merchant. He comes in June and tells you wheat will be dear, and in October it is cheap, and somehow he is never the poorer for it."

"We try to see the whole world's harvest at once. What the ships are carrying, what the granaries hold in Alexandria and in Africa, what the bakers are buying. Not to be certain — no one is certain — but so the farmer is not the last to know. And there is one more instrument, the strangest of all. It is a little oracle you keep in your hand, and you ask it questions in your own words, and it answers."

"Answers what?"

"Anything a neighbour who had read every book on farming might answer. *Why are my olive leaves curling?* *Is this the right week to graft?* *My neighbour says to plough four times and my grandfather says three.* It answers in plain speech, day or night, and it is never tired, and it never laughs at a foolish question."

Vettius is quiet. Then: "And does it know the smell of the earth after rain?"

"No."

"Then it does not know everything." He is not triumphant. He is being precise, the way a man is precise about his own trade.

---

**The objection.**

"You have made me a rich man in an afternoon," Vettius says at last. "So now I will do you the courtesy of the other argument. Who owns the little oracle? Who owns the map of my eight iugera? Because I have seen what happens when a man must borrow to buy his seed, and the lender begins to say what he may plant."

"Those are the right questions, and I will not pretend my country has answered them well. A tool that a man cannot afford, or cannot read, or does not own the fruits of, is not a tool. It is a landlord who never comes to the door."

"And the other thing." The farmer gestures at the field, the stubble, the oxen standing head to tail against the flies. "If every man in Campania plants the same wheat in the same year, because the oracle said so, then one bad month is not one man's ruin. It is everyone's."

"Also true. So the good version of this is not a voice that commands. It is a voice that whispers, and a man who still walks his own furrows."

---

**Dusk.**

The stranger rises to go. Vettius walks him to the boundary stone.

"I will tell you what I think," the farmer says. "Your instruments are better eyes and a longer memory. That is all they are, and that is not a small thing. The eye of the master fattens the land — but it must still be the master's eye. A man who stops looking at his own field because a stone is looking for him has not gained a servant. He has lost a farm."

"That," says the stranger, "is the whole of the lesson, and it took my country two hundred years and a great deal of money to learn it."

"Then your country should have asked a farmer."

---

**What the conversation shows.** Artificial intelligence does not overturn the logic of farming — read the land, husband the water, guard against blight, breed and tend the beasts, judge the season, sell wisely. It attacks the oldest constraint on all of them: that a farmer could only know what one pair of eyes, one memory, and one lifetime allowed. Sensors and imagery widen the eye to the root zone and the district; models lengthen the memory across thousands of seasons; vision systems see disease days before the eye can; forecasting and market intelligence compress the uncertainty that has always been the farmer's real crop. The Roman's objections are equally modern — cost, ownership, dependence, and the danger of everyone betting the same way — and they set the terms on which the technology actually helps: as an instrument that sharpens the master's eye, never one that replaces it.
